title: The Lungs and Respiratory System
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Biology
summary: The parts of the respiratory system, how oxygen moves from the air into the blood in the lungs, the difference between the air we breathe in and out, breathing rate and exercise, and how other vertebrates compare.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Describe the human respiratory system: oxygen from the air moves into the blood in the lungs (6Bs.02)
Know that many vertebrates have a similar system (6Bs.02)
Skills used on this page: using a model of the chest, reading bar charts and tables, repeating measurements, explaining patterns (6TWSm.01, 6TWSa.05, 6TWSc.04, 6TWSa.03)

blocks.text: Your cells need **oxygen** all the time. Oxygen is a gas in the air. The job of the **respiratory system** is to get oxygen from the air **into the blood**, and to get rid of the waste gas **carbon dioxide**. The blood (circulatory system) then carries the oxygen to every cell. The two systems always work together.

rows: Air enters here. The nose warms the air and traps dust in hairs and sticky mucus.
A tube that carries air from the throat down to the chest. Rings of cartilage keep it open.
Two tubes that carry air into the left and right lung. Inside the lungs they branch again and again into smaller tubes.
Millions of tiny bags at the ends of the smallest tubes. Here **oxygen moves into the blood**.
Two spongy organs in the chest, made of all the tubes, air sacs and capillaries.
Protect the lungs and heart; they move up and out when you breathe in.
A dome-shaped sheet of muscle under the lungs; it moves down when you breathe in.

blocks.text: **The path of air:** nose or mouth → windpipe → bronchi → smaller tubes → air sacs. To breathe out, air goes the opposite way.
How oxygen gets into the blood
Each tiny air sac is wrapped in **capillaries** (the smallest blood vessels). The wall of the air sac and the wall of the capillary are both **very thin** — only one cell thick. So:

items: **Oxygen** moves from the air in the air sac, through the thin walls, **into the blood**.
**Carbon dioxide** moves from the blood into the air sac, and is **breathed out**.
The blood, now rich in oxygen, goes to the heart, which pumps it around the body (see The Heart and Circulatory System).

blocks.text: The lungs are very good at this job because they have **millions of air sacs** (together they give a huge surface for oxygen to pass through), the walls are **very thin**, and there are **lots of capillaries** carrying blood past the air sacs all the time.

blocks.text: **How the model helps:** it shows that the diaphragm moving down makes the lungs fill with air — something we cannot see inside our body. **Its limits:** the bottle cannot move like the ribs; real lungs are not hollow balloons but are full of tiny tubes and air sacs; and there is no blood, so the model cannot show oxygen moving into the blood.
Air breathed in and air breathed out

rows: Some oxygen moved into the blood in the lungs.
Carbon dioxide moved out of the blood into the lungs.
The body does not use nitrogen gas.
Water evaporates from the moist lining of the lungs.

blocks.text: So breathed-out air has **less oxygen** and **more carbon dioxide**. Notice that breathed-out air still contains quite a lot of oxygen (about 16%) — that is why rescue breathing can help a person who has stopped breathing. Breathed-out air is also **warmer** and **wetter**: on a cold day you can see the water vapour condense as a little cloud.

**Breathing is not the same as respiration.** Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration happens inside every cell: the cell uses oxygen to release energy from nutrients and makes carbon dioxide as waste. That is why cells need oxygen and why blood must take carbon dioxide away.
Breathing rate and exercise

Your **breathing rate** is the number of breaths you take in one minute. When you exercise, your muscles need **more oxygen** to release more energy and they make **more carbon dioxide**. So you breathe **faster and deeper**, to take more oxygen into the blood and remove more carbon dioxide. At the same time your heart beats faster to carry the blood more quickly.

blocks.text: **Keeping lungs healthy:** dust and smoke can damage the tiny air sacs, so they let less oxygen into the blood. This is one reason why breathing smoke (including cigarette smoke) is harmful.
Other vertebrates

**Many vertebrates have a similar respiratory system:** mammals, birds and reptiles breathe air into **lungs**, where oxygen moves into the blood. Fish live in water, so they use **gills** instead of lungs. Water flows over the gills, and oxygen dissolved in the water moves into the blood in the gills. The job is the same — getting oxygen into the blood — only the organ is different. Frogs (amphibians) use lungs and can also take in oxygen through their thin, moist skin.

headers: Takes oxygen into the blood using…
rows: lungs (whales and dolphins come to the surface to breathe air)

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1** (the path of air)
Put these in the order air passes through them when you breathe in: air sacs, windpipe, nose, bronchi. [2]

items: **nose → windpipe → bronchi → air sacs**. 2 marks for all four in order; 1 mark if one pair is swapped.
Think of it as big to small: the windpipe is one wide tube, the bronchi are two tubes, and the air sacs are tiny.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** (where oxygen enters the blood)
Describe how oxygen from the air gets into the blood. [2]

items: Oxygen in the air reaches the **air sacs** in the **lungs** [1].
It passes through the **thin walls** of the air sacs and the capillaries into the **blood** [1].

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** "The lungs pump oxygen to the body." The lungs do not pump: oxygen moves into the blood in the lungs, and the **heart** pumps the blood.
**Worked example 3** (breathed-in and breathed-out air)
Use the table of breathed-in and breathed-out air. (a) Work out the difference in the amount of oxygen. [1] (b) Explain why breathed-out air contains more carbon dioxide. [1]

items: (a) 21% − 16% = **5%** less oxygen in breathed-out air.
(b) Carbon dioxide (waste from the cells) **moves from the blood into the air sacs** and is breathed out.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** (breathing-rate investigation)

Youssef wants to find out how the time he spends jogging affects his breathing rate. He jogs for 1, 2, 3 and 4 minutes and then counts his breaths for one minute. After jogging for 3 minutes he counts 30, 32 and 31 breaths on three different days. (a) Name the independent variable. [1] (b) Name the dependent variable. [1] (c) Work out the mean breathing rate after 3 minutes. [1] (d) Predict what happens to his breathing rate as he jogs for longer, and explain. [2]

items: (a) the **time spent jogging**
(b) the **breathing rate** (number of breaths in one minute)

(d) Prediction [1]: the breathing rate will **increase** the longer he jogs. Reason [1]: his muscles need more oxygen (and must get rid of more carbon dioxide), so he breathes faster to take more oxygen into the blood.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** (evaluating the model)
In the balloon model, what does the rubber sheet represent? Give one way the model is different from a real chest. [2]

items: The rubber sheet represents the **diaphragm** [1].
Different [1]: the bottle cannot move like the ribs / real lungs are not hollow balloons / there are no air sacs or blood in the model.

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** (other vertebrates)
A tilapia fish and a camel both need oxygen. Compare how they get oxygen into their blood. [2]

items: The camel breathes air into its **lungs**, and oxygen moves into the blood in the lungs [1].
The fish takes oxygen from **water** using its **gills**; oxygen moves into the blood in the gills [1].

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying we breathe in only oxygen and breathe out only carbon dioxide. Air breathed in and out is mostly nitrogen; breathed-out air still has about 16% oxygen.
Saying the lungs pump blood or oxygen. The heart pumps blood; oxygen moves into the blood in the lungs.
Saying the oxygen goes "into the lungs" as the full answer. The objective is that oxygen moves from the air **into the blood** in the lungs.
Mixing up the order of tubes: windpipe first, then bronchi, then air sacs.
Saying the diaphragm moves up when you breathe in. It moves **down** when you breathe in.
Saying fish have lungs. Fish use gills.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: Label a simple diagram: windpipe, lung, diaphragm, bronchus. Use the label lines carefully — the end of the line shows the part.
"Complete the sentence: Oxygen moves from the ______ into the ______ in the lungs." → air, blood.
Tables of breathed-in and breathed-out air: work out a difference and explain it.
Exercise investigations: read a bar chart of breathing rates, name the variables, explain why breathing gets faster, combine with pulse rate.
Models: "What does the rubber sheet / balloon represent?" and "Give one limitation of this model."
Other vertebrates: say which animals use lungs and that fish use gills.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: The lungs and breathing: practice
blocks.intro: 14 Checkpoint-style questions on the respiratory system. Use the diagrams, table and chart.

questions.q: In which organ does oxygen from the air move into the blood?
questions.e: Oxygen moves from the air into the blood in the lungs (in the air sacs).

questions.q: Name the tube that carries air from the throat down towards the lungs.
questions.e: The windpipe (trachea) carries air from the throat to the bronchi and lungs.

questions.q: Name the tiny bags in the lungs where oxygen passes into the blood.
questions.e: The air sacs (alveoli) have thin walls and are surrounded by capillaries, so oxygen passes into the blood there.

questions.q: Which gas moves from the blood into the air sacs to be breathed out?
questions.e: Carbon dioxide is a waste gas made by the cells. It moves from the blood into the air sacs and is breathed out.

questions.p:
Question 8
Sara counts her breathing rate after different activities. The bar chart shows her results.
questions.q: (c) Explain why Sara breathes faster when she runs.
questions.ms: 1 mark: her muscles need more oxygen / energy (OR make more carbon dioxide). 1 mark: breathing faster takes more oxygen into the blood (in the lungs) / removes more carbon dioxide. Do not accept: "she is out of breath" with no science.
questions.e: Running muscles need more oxygen to release energy, and they make more carbon dioxide. Breathing faster gets more oxygen into the blood in the lungs and gets rid of more carbon dioxide.

questions.p:
Question 12
Mr Khaled makes a model of the chest using a plastic bottle, a straw, two balloons and a rubber sheet.
questions.q: (b) Mr Khaled pulls the rubber sheet down. Describe what happens to the balloons and explain why. Then give one way the model is not like a real chest.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the balloons get bigger / inflate / fill with air. 1 mark: because the space inside the bottle gets bigger (so air comes in through the straw). 1 mark: limitation — the bottle cannot move like the ribs / real lungs are not hollow / have air sacs / there is no blood or capillaries in the model / real lungs are spongy. Accept any sensible scientific limitation.
questions.e: Pulling the sheet down (like the diaphragm moving down) makes the space in the bottle bigger, so air is drawn in through the straw and the balloons inflate. The model is not exactly like the chest: the bottle walls cannot move like ribs, and the balloons are hollow, with no air sacs or blood.

questions.q: Which animal takes oxygen into its blood using gills?
questions.e: Fish such as tilapia use gills to take oxygen from water. Pigeons, camels and lizards breathe air into lungs.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Path of air: nose/mouth → windpipe (trachea) → bronchi → air sacs in the lungs.
In the air sacs, oxygen moves from the air into the blood; carbon dioxide moves out of the blood and is breathed out.
Air sacs work well because there are millions of them, their walls are very thin, and they are surrounded by capillaries.
Breathed-out air has less oxygen (about 16%) and more carbon dioxide (about 4%) than breathed-in air.
Exercise → muscles need more oxygen → faster, deeper breathing (and a faster heartbeat).
Many vertebrates (mammals, birds, reptiles) breathe with lungs; fish use gills to get oxygen into their blood.
